Another indication of income is a comparison of poverty levels.

According to the 1970 U.S. Census poverty index, 39.4 percent of resident Crow Indian familites are in poverty. By comparison, 21.4 percent of all families in Big Horn County and 10.4 percent for all of Montana are below the poverty level. The on-reservation median family income for the Crow Indians in 1969 was $5,260 compared to $8,210 for the white families on the reservation. 1/
The BIA (BIA, Labor Force Report, April, 1975) reports a total of 580 on-reservation Crow individuals who earn more than $5,000 per year from full or part-time employment and 345 who earn less than $5,000 per year.
Labor Force and Employment
Table II-19 shows that in 1970, of 1,686 Indians and 4,814 whites age 16 years or older, 38.9 percent of the Indians and 58.3 percent of the whites were in the labor force. There were 340 males and 690 female Indians not in the labor force, and 432 white males and 1,577 white females in the same category. For census analyses, the labor force is defined as those 16 years old or older employed or actively seeking work. Many of those not in the labor force are 65 years old or older, are housewives, or are students. If bona fide employment opportunities existed, a considerable number of those not presently in the labor force probably would accept work. The actual number would depend upon training conditions, wages, working conditions and living conditions, among other factors (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 c).
The nation-wide poverty threshold for a farm family of four headed by a male was $3,197, while for a family of 6.16 (the average size of Crow families in poverty) the index was approximately $4,500.
